section.title: The Church at Antioch
section.sectionRationale: The believers scattered by Stephen's persecution reach Antioch, and some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, take the daring step of preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks as well as Jews. A great number believe, and a new kind of church is born, made of Jew and Gentile together. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who rejoices, fetches Saul, and teaches for a year, and here the disciples are first called Christians. When famine looms, this young church sends relief back to Judea, showing a family bound across every barrier.
section.thesis: At Antioch the gospel deliberately crosses to the Greeks and creates a thriving mixed church of Jew and Gentile, encouraged by Barnabas and taught by Saul, so that a new missionary base is formed, the name Christian is first given, and the grace received flows out in generosity to others.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the gospel preached to the Greeks at Antioch and many believing; Barnabas sent and rejoicing at the grace of God; Barnabas fetching Saul, a year of teaching, and the name Christian; and the church sending famine relief to Judea.

units.label: The gospel reaches the Greeks at Antioch
units.note: a great number believe and turn to the Lord

verses.text: Meanwhile those scattered by the persecution that began with Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the message only to Jews.
But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, went to Antioch and began speaking to the {{hellen|Greeks}} as well, proclaiming the good news about the Lord Jesus.
The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number of people believed and {{epistrepho|turned}} to the Lord.

units.label: Barnabas sent to Antioch
units.note: he saw the grace of God and rejoiced

verses.text: When news of this reached the ears of the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch.
When he arrived and saw the {{charis|grace}} of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to abide in the Lord with all their hearts.
Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord.

units.label: Barnabas fetches Saul, and disciples are called Christians
units.note: a year of teaching in a mixed church

verses.text: Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul,

and when he found him, he brought him back to Antioch. So for a full year they met together with the church and taught large numbers of people. The disciples were first called {{christianos|Christians}} at Antioch.

units.label: Famine relief for Judea
units.note: grace received flows out in generosity

verses.text: In those days some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them named Agabus stood up and predicted through the Spirit that a great famine would sweep across the whole world. (This happened under Claudius.)
So the disciples, each according to his ability, decided to send relief to the brothers living in Judea.
This they did, sending their gifts to the elders with Barnabas and Saul.

hellen.gloss: A Greek, and more broadly a Gentile by culture, a non-Jew. That the scattered believers began preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks as well as Jews marks a deliberate step across the old divide and the birth of a mixed church at Antioch.

epistrepho.gloss: To turn around, to turn back, to convert. The great number who turned to the Lord describes real conversion, a decisive turning from idols and self to the living Christ, the fruit of the hand of the Lord being with the preachers.

charis.gloss: Grace, the undeserved favor and kindness of God. Barnabas saw the grace of God, not merely human enthusiasm, in the changed lives at Antioch, and it was this evidence of grace that made him rejoice and call them to hold fast to the Lord.

christianos.gloss: Christian, one belonging to or identified with Christ. First given at Antioch, likely by outsiders, the name captures what the church is: a people so marked by Christ that His name becomes their name.

basic.context: The believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen carry the gospel north to Antioch, a great mixed city. At first they speak only to Jews, but some bolder men begin telling Greeks about the Lord Jesus too, and many believe. Jerusalem sends Barnabas to check on it; he sees God's grace at work, rejoices, and encourages them. He then fetches Saul from Tarsus, and together they teach the church for a year. Here the disciples are first called Christians. When a famine is predicted, the church sends relief to Judea. The key questions are: why is preaching to the Greeks so significant, what does Barnabas model, and why does grace lead to generosity.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the next stage after the Cornelius breakthrough: what God did once at Caesarea now becomes an ongoing, deliberate mission to Gentiles, producing a whole church. Watch the pattern of grace: God's hand brings people to faith, a mature encourager nurtures them, sound teaching establishes them, and the fruit is a new identity and outward-flowing love. The naming Christian and the famine gift are signs of a healthy, maturing church.
basic.originalLanguages: The daring move is to preach to Hellen, Greeks, and not Jews only. A great number epistrepho, turn, to the Lord in genuine conversion. Barnabas sees the charis, the grace, of God among them and rejoices. And the disciples are first called Christianos, Christians, those belonging to Christ. The words trace a mixed church born of grace and marked by Christ's own name.
basic.typology: Antioch begins to reverse the scattering of the nations, gathering Jew and Greek into one worshipping community. The name Christian anticipates the new humanity in Christ that Paul will describe. The famine offering foreshadows the pattern of grace producing generosity that runs through the New Testament collections.
basic.christ: The message is simply the Lord Jesus, and it is the hand of the Lord that makes it fruitful. The church is defined by Christ so fully that His people take His name. Everything good here, the conversions, the grace, the teaching, the generosity, flows from union with the risen Lord who is building His church among the nations.
basic.god: God's grace is the engine of the whole account. His hand is with the preachers, His grace is visible in changed lives, and His Spirit speaks through the prophet Agabus. Barnabas, full of the Spirit and faith, is God's gift to steady the young church. The story shows God building His people and providing for them through one another.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 13 shows Antioch becoming the launch point of Paul's missionary journeys. Acts 4 introduces Barnabas as the son of encouragement. Galatians 2 recalls Antioch's importance and its tensions. 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 develop the grace that overflows in generous giving.
basic.oneStory: Antioch is where the church of the nations comes of age. A mixed people, first called Christians, becomes a base from which the gospel will go to the ends of the earth. The grace they received turns outward in love, and the whole movement of Acts, from Jerusalem to the world, gathers momentum here.

context.literary:
Acts 11:19 restarts a thread Luke dropped at 8:4. There he told us that those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went; here he picks the same thread up with nearly the same opening words and follows it to its first great result. In between he has told of Saul's conversion, Peter's ministry on the coast, and the Cornelius breakthrough. The effect is that Antioch is not a new story but the delayed answer to Stephen's death: the persecution of 8:1 scattered the church, and the scattering has now reached the third city of the empire.

The passage moves in three short scenes, each set off by a change of place. Verses 19 to 21 are spontaneous and unofficial: unnamed men, no apostle, no commission, and the only explanation Luke offers is the hand of the Lord. Verses 22 to 26 bring the official church in, as Jerusalem sends Barnabas and Barnabas in turn sends himself to Tarsus for Saul. Verses 27 to 30 close the circle with a prophecy and a gift. Notice the traffic. Prophets come down from Jerusalem to Antioch, and relief goes back from Antioch to Jerusalem, carried by the same two men who will soon be sent out from Antioch to the world. Gifts of word and gifts of money run in both directions.

Luke also controls the numbers. A great number believed, verse 21, and a great number were brought to the Lord, verse 24, and large numbers were taught, verse 26. The phrase comes round three times in seven verses, and it is set beside a quiet portrait of one man, Barnabas, whom Luke bothers to describe in a full verse. The passage is a growth report built around a person.

Finally, note what Luke leaves unsaid. He does not tell us the names of the first Greek preachers beyond their homelands, and he does not record a single sermon. The point is not their technique but the Lord's hand and the church's response.
context.historical:
Antioch on the Orontes was founded around 300 BC by Seleucus I and became the capital of the Seleucid kingdom and later of the Roman province of Syria. Ancient writers rank it behind Rome and Alexandria. It sat about fifteen miles inland from the Mediterranean, with the port of Seleucia serving it, which is why Barnabas and Saul will later go down to Seleucia to sail, 13:4. It was a trade city on a major road, famously cosmopolitan, with a large Jewish community that had enjoyed settled civic standing for generations. A man named Nicolas, a convert to Judaism from Antioch, was among the seven chosen alongside Stephen, 6:5, so the church in Jerusalem already had a link to the city.

The founding preachers came from Cyprus and Cyrene, a Mediterranean island and a Greek city on the North African coast. Both had Jewish populations and both sent pilgrims to Jerusalem. Barnabas himself was a Levite from Cyprus, 4:36, and Lucius of Cyrene will be named among the Antioch leaders, 13:1. These were Greek-speaking Jews at home in two worlds, which is exactly the profile of people who would cross the line to Gentile neighbours.

The famine comes under Claudius, who reigned from AD 41 to 54. Roman writers record grain shortages in his reign, and the Jewish historian Josephus describes a severe famine in Judea in the 40s when Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from abroad to relieve it. A Jewish province already near the edge, with a church that had shared its goods in the early days and whose members were often poor, 2:44 to 45, would have felt such a shortage at once.

The gift goes to the elders, verse 30, which is the first time Luke mentions the elders of the Jerusalem church. The apostles are no longer the only visible leaders, and money for the poor is handed to local oversight. Saul's years in Tarsus, verse 25, are a quiet gap. He had been sent home there for safety, 9:30, and tells the Galatians that he then went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, Galatians 1:21.
context.canonical:
The scattering of 8:1 fulfils, in a way no one planned, the programme Jesus gave in 1:8: Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth. Acts 11:19 names Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch as stations on the way out. Antioch then becomes the centre from which the mission in the rest of Acts goes, sending Paul and Barnabas in 13:1 to 3 and receiving them back in 14:26 to 28. Acts 15:35 shows both still teaching there after the Jerusalem council.

The passage also runs on the track laid by Cornelius. In 11:1 to 18 Peter defends the Gentile conversions to a sceptical Jerusalem church, and the verdict is that God has granted repentance leading to life to the Gentiles. Verse 19 begins as if that debate had settled nothing, since the scattered speak only to Jews, and then verse 20 shows the principle at work. Gentile faith is first a Spirit-given exception, then a settled pattern.

Antioch will also be a place of testing. Paul recounts the clash with Peter and even Barnabas over table fellowship, Galatians 2:11 to 14, and Acts 15:1 to 2 tells of men from Judea teaching that Gentiles must be circumcised. The same church that gave birth to the Gentile mission is where the question of its terms becomes sharp.

The relief for Judea sets the pattern for the longest running appeal in Paul's letters. He directs the Galatian and Corinthian churches to set aside money weekly for Jerusalem, 1 Corinthians 16:1 to 3, praises the Macedonians for giving out of poverty, 2 Corinthians 8:1 to 2, and explains the logic in Romans 15:26 and 27: those who shared in Israel's spiritual blessings owe material blessings in return. And the name Christian, rare in the New Testament, appears again on the lips of Agrippa, 26:28, and in Peter's call to bear it without shame, 1 Peter 4:16.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see that the Gentile church was not a plan Jerusalem drew up but a work God did through ordinary refugees, and that Jerusalem then did the right thing with it. The sequence is deliberate. First God acts, with a hand on the preaching and a great number turning. Then the mother church investigates, and sends not an inspector but an encourager who looks at what has happened and recognises grace. Then the work is steadied by teaching, a full year of it, with two leaders working side by side. Finally the church's maturity shows in its giving.

For first readers who were wondering whether a church made up mostly of Gentiles was legitimate, the passage is an argument by narrative. The Jerusalem apostles did not create it, but they blessed it, and its first act of fellowship was to feed them. For later readers it is a pattern of healthy church growth: evangelism that crosses lines, oversight that rejoices rather than polices, teaching that goes deep, and giving that goes outward. Luke does not say the church was perfect, and Galatians 2 will show it was not, but he wants us to see what grace looks like when it is given room.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything here is description: who went where, who was sent, what a prophet said, how much was given. Luke does not command that churches be planted by refugees, that a famine be met with a collection, or that a church be led by two men. Some details are simply historical. The disciples gave each according to ability, verse 29, and Luke gives no figure and no percentage, so the passage cannot be turned into a tithe formula.

The prescriptive weight comes from the way Luke commends what he describes. He calls Barnabas a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, verse 24, and sets him up as a model without issuing a command. He notes that the giving was voluntary and proportionate, which agrees with the plain commands Paul later gives in 2 Corinthians 9:7. Treat the narrative as a pattern to be tested against the direct teaching of the epistles, and take from it what they confirm: cross-cultural witness, encouragement that makes no demands the gospel does not, generosity that crosses borders, and respect between churches.

debates.question: To whom did the men from Cyprus and Cyrene preach, Greek-speaking Jews or Gentile Greeks?

views.label: Gentile Greeks, marking a new step beyond the Jews
views.case: The strongest case reads the Greeks as Gentiles, since Luke contrasts them in verse 20 with the Jews spoken to in verse 19, and the whole point is that the scattered believers now went further than before. The astonishment, the sending of Barnabas from Jerusalem, and the new mixed church that results all fit a deliberate turn to Gentiles, building on the Cornelius breakthrough.

views.label: Greek-speaking Jews or God-fearers only
views.case: A minority reads the word as Hellenists, Greek-speaking Jews, partly because manuscripts divide between two similar forms of the word. This respects a real textual question, but it blunts Luke's clear contrast with verse 19 and the significance he plainly attaches to what happened at Antioch.

debates.bearing: Taking the Greeks as Gentiles fits Luke's storyline that the gospel is now crossing to the nations in an ongoing way, and explains why Antioch becomes the mother church of the Gentile mission.

debates.question: Who gave the believers the name Christians, and was it meant kindly?

views.label: Outsiders, perhaps as a mocking label
views.case: The name appears only three times in the New Testament, here, in Acts 26:28 on the lips of Agrippa, and in 1 Peter 4:16, where it is tied to suffering and shame. In each case it is outsiders or persecution that make it fit. The ending of the word marks a follower or partisan of a person, as a political label would. On this reading, Antioch's pagan neighbours coined it, and the church later wore it with pride.

views.label: God's own naming of His people
views.case: The verb Luke uses can mean to be called, as in Romans 7:3, but elsewhere in the New Testament it also carries the sense of divine instruction or warning, as in Acts 10:22 where an angel instructs Cornelius. Some therefore take the name as given by God, in line with the promise that His people would be called by His name, Isaiah 43:7. The verb alone cannot settle it.

views.label: The believers themselves
views.case: A few suggest the disciples chose the name, but the New Testament writers otherwise call themselves disciples, brothers, saints and believers, which weighs against it.

debates.bearing: Whoever coined it, Luke records it as a fact about identity: at Antioch the church could no longer be understood as a Jewish party and was seen as a people defined by Christ. Peter's word in 1 Peter 4:16 shows what to do with a name that may cost something.

debates.question: Is the famine visit of 11:30 the same Jerusalem visit as Galatians 2:1 to 10?

views.label: Yes, Galatians 2 describes this visit
views.case: If Paul in Galatians lists every visit to Jerusalem that could bear on his independence, the famine trip, 11:30 and 12:25, is his second, and the Jerusalem council is an event after Galatians was written. This resolves the apparent gap, since Galatians does not mention the council at all.

views.label: No, Galatians 2 matches the council of Acts 15
views.case: Others note the private meeting, the discussion of Titus and circumcision, and the agreement about Gentile mission, all of which look like the council. On this view the famine visit goes unmentioned because it had nothing to do with Paul's argument.

debates.bearing: The question does not touch the point of 11:27 to 30, which is that the Gentile church sent aid to the Jewish church, but readers should know it is open.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke's vocabulary here is small and carefully chosen. Start with the instruction Barnabas gives in verse 23, to abide in the Lord with all their hearts. The verb is prosmeno, to stay with, to remain attached to, and Luke uses it again in 13:43 where Paul and Barnabas urge the new believers to continue in the grace of God. It is the ordinary word for holding fast. Joined to it is the phrase translated 'with all their hearts', which literally speaks of a purpose of the heart, prothesis. Barnabas is not asking for a mood but for a settled resolve, the kind a person makes once and then lives in. Notice that the encouragement does not ask them to join anything; it asks them to stay where grace has already placed them.

The verb for encouraged, parakaleo, is the root behind the nickname Luke gave in 4:36, 'Son of Encouragement', parakleseos. The same verb can mean to comfort, to urge, to exhort, even to plead, and the context here makes it the strong and warm kind. Luke is making a small joke with his readers. The man called the Son of Encouragement does what his name says, at the one moment when the church's future hung on whether Jerusalem would frown or rejoice.

In verse 20 the good news is preached with the verb euangelizo, proclaimed as good news, and its object is not 'the word' as in 8:4 but the Lord Jesus. The title kyrios in a Greek city is loaded. To a Gentile ear the word could name a master, a ruler, even an emperor, and these Gentiles hear Jesus offered to them under the title Peter gave in Acts 10:36, Lord of all. The accompanying clause in verse 21, the hand of the Lord was with them, uses a phrase that Luke has used at the birth of John, Luke 1:66, and which echoes the Old Testament idiom for God's powerful intervention. It is God acting, not the evangelists' skill.

The word for what Barnabas saw, in verse 23, is the grace of God. It is something visible. The Greek verb is simply eidon, he saw, and Luke does not say what he saw. The reader is invited to imagine changed lives, shared meals, Jews and Greeks together. The grace is not an abstract doctrine here but a sight that makes a man glad.

Finally, the word for the relief in verse 29 is diakonia, service, ministry, the same word group Luke has used for the daily distribution of food in Acts 6:1 and 6:2. The Antioch church's gift is thus placed in the same category as the work the seven were appointed to do, and the word will be used of the collection again in Romans 15:31 and 2 Corinthians 9:1. Giving to need is ministry.

typology.type: One flock from two folds, John 10:16
typology.fulfillment: Jesus told His disciples, 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd.' Antioch is the first large and visible fulfilment: Greeks who had never been in Israel's fold hear the Shepherd's voice and are gathered in with Jews. Paul explains the doctrine behind it, that Christ made the two one and tore down the dividing wall, Ephesians 2:14. The picture is incomplete at Antioch, as Galatians 2:11 to 14 shows, and it will be finished only when a multitude from every nation stands before the Lamb, Revelation 7:9.

typology.type: Nations bringing wealth to Zion, answered in reverse
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foresaw the day when 'the wealth of the nations will come to you,' Isaiah 60:5, a promise about Gentile riches flowing to Jerusalem. At Antioch something like it begins, but the shape is new. The Gentile church sends relief as a love gift to poor believers, not tribute to a city, and Paul reads it the same way, saying that those who shared in the spiritual blessings of the Jews ought to share material ones, Romans 15:27. The pattern also echoes Genesis 41:57, when every nation came to Joseph for grain, but now the bread flows toward the family that first shared the gospel. The type falls short in that Jerusalem is not the final destination; the gifts go to people, not to a temple.

typology.type: The name carried by God's people
typology.fulfillment: God told Moses that Aaron and his sons would 'put My name on the Israelites,' Numbers 6:27, and Isaiah speaks of 'everyone called by My name and created for My glory,' Isaiah 43:7. At Antioch a name is attached to a people again, but now it is the name of Christ, the Anointed One. The pattern escalates because the people are no longer defined by one nation but by one Lord, and it is carried by Jews and Greeks alike. Peter says that to bear it is to glorify God, 1 Peter 4:16. The correspondence is a pattern of identity and not a prediction. A name can be worn emptily, and Jesus warns of people who say 'Lord, Lord' without knowing Him, Matthew 7:21.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most plainly by what it says the Greeks heard. They were not offered a philosophy or a better set of customs but 'the good news about the Lord Jesus,' verse 20. John records a moment in the last week of Jesus' life when some Greeks came to Philip and said, 'Sir, we want to see Jesus,' John 12:20 to 21, and Jesus answered by speaking of a kernel of wheat that must fall into the ground and die to bear much fruit, John 12:24. Acts 11 is the harvest of that grain. Stephen fell, the church was scattered like seed, and Greeks in Antioch saw Jesus through the lips of those who had known Him.

It leads to Christ by promise. Jesus told His disciples that He had other sheep who would hear His voice and join one flock under one shepherd, John 10:16, and He told them they would be witnesses to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8. Verse 21 reads like the fulfilment: the hand of the Lord was with them and a great number turned. The work belongs to the exalted Lord, who is still building His church from heaven, as Matthew 16:18 promised.

It leads to Christ in the church's very name. Christos means Anointed One, and the one who was anointed with the Holy Spirit and power, Acts 10:38, has a people who are now known by Him. The name is not a badge of membership in a movement but a statement of belonging.

It also leads to Christ by pattern in the way the church gives. Paul presses the Corinthians to give by pointing to the Lord: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The Antioch gift is a small echo of that descent. And Jesus identified Himself with His hungry people, 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' Matthew 25:40, so the grain sent to Judea is, in His own reckoning, grain given to Him.

Be careful not to press the details. Barnabas going to Tarsus for Saul is not a picture of Christ seeking the lost, and Agabus standing up is not a type. The links above rest on what Jesus Himself said and what the apostles say about giving. The passage is not about Christ's person in any hidden way; it shows the effect of the Lord's reign over a city, and it shows His body doing what He did.
study.god:
God is the first actor in this passage and the last. Luke never says that the refugees decided to evangelise Greeks and succeeded; he says the hand of the Lord was with them. That is a statement about God's sovereignty in the use of suffering. The persecution that began with Stephen's death was a human crime, and Luke does not excuse it. Yet God used the dispersal to carry the message further than any plan could have. Joseph's words to his brothers fit: 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this,' Genesis 50:20. Antioch is a day like this, and it comes straight out of a day of violence.

He is a God of grace that can be seen. Barnabas sees the grace of God, verse 23, and the sight settles the matter for him. The Lord who gave the Holy Spirit to Cornelius's household has now given repentance and faith to a great number of Greeks, and no one in Jerusalem can honestly doubt it. God authenticates His own work by its fruit, and the right response is to rejoice rather than investigate for flaws.

He is a God who speaks ahead of events. The Spirit foretold the famine through Agabus, verse 28, so that the church could prepare. He is not careless of material need. The prophecy leads to no panic but to generous planning, with each giving according to ability, which means God's foreknowledge is given to his people to serve others, not to alarm them. Agabus appears again in Acts 21:10 to 11 with another prophecy, which suggests that Luke is quietly showing a gift of the Spirit that works across time.

He is a God who builds through people. He uses nameless refugees, a man known for encouragement, a convert from Tarsus who waited years, and a congregation of both Jews and Greeks. Luke writes that Barnabas was full of the Holy Spirit and faith, verse 24, and that is what the Spirit-filled life looks like in a leader: gladness over others' success and willingness to share the work. God does not need the church's polish, only its availability.

For worship, the passage invites gladness rather than anxiety. If the work is the hand of the Lord, then the church's task is to rejoice where grace is visible, to hold fast to Him with settled hearts, and to share what it has. The God who orders scattering and famine is the God who gathers a people from every nation, and the song around His throne, Revelation 7:9, begins in cities like Antioch.

crossReferences.note: The first scattering. Luke picks up here almost word for word at 11:19, so Antioch is the long-delayed result of Stephen's death. What the persecutors meant to crush spread the word, which is why the passage reads as an answer to a question the reader has carried since chapter 8.

Barnabas is introduced as Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. The man whom the apostles named Son of Encouragement is the one sent to Antioch, so his generosity and his encouragement are the same character at work, in Jerusalem and now in Antioch.

Earlier it was Barnabas who vouched for Saul when the Jerusalem church feared him, and Saul was sent away to Tarsus. In 11:25 to 26 Barnabas goes and finds him, showing that the encourager spots gifts in others and remembers them across years.

Peter's defence of Cornelius's baptism ends in the conclusion that God has granted repentance leading to life even to the Gentiles. Antioch shows the principle becoming a pattern, which is why Jerusalem's response in verse 22 is to send help rather than to challenge.

Antioch's leaders are listed, including Barnabas, Lucius of Cyrene and Saul, and the Spirit sends two of them out. The church that received Gentiles in chapter 11 becomes the church that goes to the Gentiles in chapter 13, with the same two men.

Paul remembers the day Peter and even Barnabas drew back from eating with Gentiles at Antioch. It is a sober footnote to the joy of Acts 11. The unity of Jew and Greek in one church was real and was not automatic, and it needed the truth of the gospel to hold.

Paul explains why the Gentile churches give to Jerusalem: since the Gentiles shared in the Jews' spiritual blessings, they owe them material ones. This puts words to what the Antioch disciples did by instinct, and ties generosity to the debt of gospel gratitude.

The Macedonians gave out of deep poverty and joy, and Paul grounds all giving in the grace of the Lord Jesus, who was rich and became poor. It reads as a commentary on Antioch, where grace received overflowed in grace given.

Peter speaks of suffering as a Christian and says not to be ashamed but to glorify God in that name. It is the best commentary on how the early church took the name first used at Antioch, whether or not it began as an insult.

Jesus spoke of other sheep not of this fold whom He must bring in so that there will be one flock. Antioch is the first big gathering of those sheep, as Greeks hear His voice through scattered preachers.

Greeks came wanting to see Jesus, and He answered with a saying about a grain of wheat that dies and bears much fruit. The scattering of the church after Stephen is that grain in the ground, and Antioch is the fruit.
Agabus appears again with a prophecy about Paul's arrest. Luke wants the reader to remember the man who warned of famine and so see that the Spirit's word through him was reliable then and later.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with one human family and a blessing meant for all nations, and then the nations scatter at Babel, Genesis 11:8 to 9, their languages divided. God's answer is to call Abraham so that in him all the families of the earth might be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Nearly everything in the Old Testament that follows is that promise being carried slowly toward its goal, through Israel's law, kings and prophets, with glimpses of nations coming to the light, Isaiah 60:3, and of a servant who would be a light to the Gentiles, Isaiah 49:6.

Acts 11 is where the answer to Babel first becomes visible as a community. Greeks and Jews, from Cyprus, Cyrene and Antioch itself, sit in one church and are taught together for a year. They do not speak one language; they confess one Lord. Pentecost, Acts 2, had already shown the scattering of tongues turned toward understanding, and Cornelius had shown that the Spirit does not wait for circumcision. Antioch shows what happens when that becomes a settled life: a multi-ethnic congregation with teachers, prophets, a name, and a budget.

The passage also sits in the long line of famine stories that mark the people of God. Famine drove Abraham to Egypt, Genesis 12:10, Jacob's family to Joseph, Genesis 41 to 47, Naomi to Moab, Ruth 1:1. In each, God used scarcity to move His people. Here the famine is turned into a channel for love between two halves of the church, and that bond of mutual giving becomes a visible sign of the one body Paul will describe in Ephesians 2.

What Antioch sets up is the mission of the rest of Acts and of the church's history. From this city Paul and Barnabas will go out in chapter 13, and from the same city the council question will go up to Jerusalem in chapter 15. The tension between Jew and Gentile, and the resolution that salvation is by grace through faith, is worked out in the shadow of this church.

It ends in the new creation, where the multitude that no one could count stands before the throne 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9. The first stirrings of that crowd are in Antioch, where people from different homelands are first called by one name. There will be no more famine, no more need of relief, and no more division at the table, for the nations will walk by the light of the Lamb, Revelation 21:24.

sermon.title: The Gospel Church (Acts 11:19-30; 13:1-3)
sermon.why: Keller preaches the Antioch church directly from this passage, drawing out Barnabas's ministry of encouragement, the grace of God at work, and how a healthy gospel church grows and reaches outward, matching the heart of this study.

quiz.q: What was the significant new step taken by the believers at Antioch?

options.text: They began preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks as well as Jews, forming a mixed church.
options.note: Verse 20 marks the deliberate turn to the Greeks, building on the Gentile breakthrough.

options.text: They preached the gospel in a large and important Gentile city.
options.note: True and part of the significance, but the key step was reaching the Greeks, not merely the location.

options.text: They began organizing the church with elders and prophets.
options.note: Prophets appear and elders are mentioned, but the defining new step was preaching to the Greeks.

options.text: They stopped preaching to Jews altogether.
options.note: They preached to Greeks as well as Jews; they did not abandon the Jews.

quiz.q: What did Barnabas see when he arrived at Antioch, and how did he respond?

options.text: He saw the grace of God, rejoiced, and encouraged them to hold fast to the Lord.
options.note: Verse 23 describes exactly this response to the evidence of grace.

options.text: He saw a large and growing crowd and was pleased at the numbers.
options.note: This mistakes mere size for the grace of God that Barnabas actually discerned.

options.text: He saw genuine faith taking root and worked to strengthen it.
options.note: Close and true, but the text specifically says he saw the grace of God and rejoiced.

options.text: He saw disorder and moved quickly to correct their errors.
options.note: He found grace to rejoice over, not error to correct.

quiz.q: Why did Barnabas go to Tarsus to find Saul?

options.text: To bring him to help teach the growing church at Antioch for a year.
options.note: Verses 25 and 26 show Barnabas fetching Saul to teach the church together.

options.text: To give the gifted Saul a role suited to his abilities.
options.note: Saul was indeed gifted, but the stated purpose was the teaching and building up of the Antioch church.

options.text: To reconcile Saul with the Jerusalem apostles.
options.note: That reconciliation had already happened earlier through Barnabas; here the aim is teaching at Antioch.

options.text: To remove Saul from ministry for a season.
options.note: The opposite is true; Barnabas drew Saul into a fruitful year of ministry.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the name Christian first being given at Antioch?

options.text: The disciples were so marked by Christ that His name became their name.
options.note: The name Christianos means those belonging to Christ, capturing the church's identity.

options.text: It gave the church a convenient label to distinguish it from Judaism.
options.note: It did distinguish them, but the deeper meaning is belonging to Christ, not mere labeling.

options.text: It showed the believers had chosen a proud title for themselves.
options.note: The name was likely given by outsiders and expresses identity in Christ, not self-promotion.

options.text: It meant the church had left behind its Jewish roots entirely.
options.note: The church remained rooted in Israel's Scriptures and Messiah; the name marks belonging to Christ, not a break from all that.

quiz.q: How did the Antioch church respond to the prophecy of a coming famine?

options.text: Each according to his ability sent relief to the brothers in Judea.
options.note: Verses 29 and 30 record this generous, organized response.

options.text: They gathered resources to protect themselves from the famine.
options.note: They gave outward to others in need rather than only securing themselves.

options.text: They sent help to fellow believers who would be affected.
options.note: True in substance, but the fuller point is that each gave according to ability, a picture of grace overflowing.

options.text: They doubted the prophecy and did nothing.
options.note: They believed Agabus and acted at once with generous relief.

questions: The believers at Antioch took the bold step of speaking about Jesus to people outside their own group. Who is outside your usual circle that God may be calling you to reach?
Barnabas rejoiced when he saw the grace of God in others. When did you last celebrate God's work in someone else's life rather than compare or compete?
Barnabas invested a year teaching new believers alongside Saul. Who is God calling you to encourage and help grow, and who has done that for you?
The disciples were first called Christians, marked out as belonging to Christ. Would those around you name you by your likeness to Jesus, and where do you long to reflect Him more?
The grace the Antioch church received overflowed into generosity toward the poor in Judea. How might the grace you have received turn outward into practical love for others in need?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered Greeks has a manuscript variant reading Hellenists, that is Greek-speaking Jews. The BSB follows the reading Greeks, meaning Gentiles, which fits Luke's contrast with verse 19 where the message went only to Jews; the footnote records the alternative.
The name Christians, Christianoi, appears only three times in the New Testament and was likely first coined by outsiders in Antioch; it means those belonging to or identified with Christ.
The phrase rendered the whole world can also mean the entire Roman world, as the BSB footnote notes; the famine under Claudius is recorded by ancient historians in the mid first century.
